The posterior in \eqref{eq:working-posterior} combines the
observation likelihood with the channel and activity priors.
Following the turbo message-passing framework in \cite{cai2026},
we separate their contributions into linear estimation and joint
denoising, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:receiver-structure}.
Linear estimation combines the received pilots with a Gaussian
input message to estimate $\mathbf X$. Joint denoising uses the
channel prior $q_{\rm tr}$ and activity prior $\rho$ to estimate
each $X_k=\alpha_kH_k$. The two estimates are exchanged through
Gaussian extrinsic messages obtained by expectation propagation
\cite{minka2001}.

The input to linear estimation is a Gaussian message from joint
denoising. Its mean
matrix is denoted by
$\mathbf X^{\rm pri}\in\mathbb C^{KN\times MN}$ and the
covariance of each column by $\gamma\I_{KN}$, with $\gamma>0$.
For each column, multiplying this message by the likelihood in
\eqref{eq:working-posterior} gives a Gaussian posterior. The
corresponding mean matrix and per-column covariance are
\cite[Sec.~III-A]{cai2026}:

The scalar $t_{\rm L}$ averages the posterior variance over
the $KN$ coefficients in a column. In our model, the phase
rotations in $\widehat{\mathbf A}$ can destroy the row
orthogonality of the pilots. We therefore retain the full matrix
in these expressions; the partial-orthogonality simplification
used in \cite[Sec.~III-A]{cai2026} does not generally apply.

For message exchange, the posterior covariance is approximated
by $t_{\rm L}\I_{KN}$ \cite{ma2015,cai2026}. Dividing the
Gaussian posterior with this covariance by the input message
removes the information supplied by joint denoising \cite{minka2001}.

Reorganizing $\mathbf R_{\rm L}$ by device gives the tensor
inputs to joint denoising, with common variance $v_{\rm L}$.

The relation $X_k=\alpha_kH_k$ couples the channel and device
activity. Following \cite[Sec.~III-B]{cai2026}, we
calculate the channel estimate conditioned on activity and the
activity probability separately, then combine them to estimate
$X_k$. Let $R_k$ and $v$ denote the input mean and variance.
The Gaussian input message defines the local observation model

Here $m=m(R,v)$ in the covariance integral. The conditional
mean is the MMSE channel estimate under the active hypothesis;
the covariance describes its estimation uncertainty. Both depend
on the full channel prior, so the dependence among the entries
of $H_k$ is retained in the posterior calculation. We denote
the approximations to $m(R_k,v)$ and
$\tr\bm\Sigma_H(R_k,v)/D$ by $\mu_k$ and $t_k$, respectively.

Activity detection compares the hypotheses $R_k=W_k$ and
$R_k=H_k+W_k$. Integrating over the channel in the active case
gives $q_{1,v}$, while the inactive likelihood $q_{0,v}$ is

Thus, the posterior activity probability depends on how well
the observation is explained by each hypothesis. Let $p_k$
denote the approximation to $p^\star(R_k,v)$ used in the

equal to $H_k$. Averaging the conditional channel moments

The first covariance term represents channel uncertainty under
the active hypothesis. The second accounts for uncertainty in

\cite[Secs.~III-C--III-D]{liu2018}, \cite[Sec.~III-B]{cai2026}.
Approximating the active-channel posterior by a Gaussian with
mean $\mu_k$ and covariance $t_k\I_D$ gives the

For the spatial covariance, write the entries of $\mu_k$ as

Averaging its trace over devices and antennas gives the scalar

The feedback uses a Gaussian approximation with mean
$\widehat X_k$ and common variance $\overline t_X$.
Let $b=\overline t_X/v$. Dividing this approximation by the

For $0<b<1$, this message has a finite, positive variance.
Reorganizing its means into $\mathbf X^{\rm pri}$ and using
$\gamma_{\rm out}$ as the input variance closes the iteration.

Evaluating these updates requires the conditional channel moments
in \eqref{eq:conditional-channel-integrals} and the activity
probability in \eqref{eq:local-activity}. The underlying integrals
over the full channel prior generally have no closed-form
expressions. Section~\ref{sec:learning} develops methods for
learning these quantities from channel samples, and
Section~\ref{sec:overall} incorporates them into the complete
receiver algorithm.

The conditional channel moments in
\eqref{eq:conditional-channel-integrals} involve integrals over
the full channel prior. Score-based representations of these
moments allow them to be obtained from a learned denoising function
\cite[Sec.~IV-A]{cai2026}. We establish these relations and derive
a training objective that includes colored Gaussian perturbations.
The activity probability in \eqref{eq:local-activity} is then
obtained by learning the density ratio between the two activity
hypotheses.

Consider the channel observation under the active hypothesis in
\eqref{eq:pseudo-awgn}. To include correlated perturbations, let
$\mathbf h_{\mathbb R}\in\mathbb R^{2D}$ concatenate the real
and imaginary parts of $\vect(H)$, with $H\sim q_{\rm tr}$.
For an independent proper complex Gaussian perturbation with
covariance $C\succ0$, the real observation is

The gradient $\nabla_{\mathbf u}\log q_{\bm\Sigma}^{\mathbb R}$
is the first-order score function. It determines the correction
to the noisy observation needed for MMSE denoising. For
$C=v\I_D$, \eqref{eq:tweedie-mean} gives the real representation
of the conditional mean in \eqref{eq:conditional-channel-integrals}.

The conditional covariance
$\mathbf P_{\mathbb R}=\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf h_{\mathbb R}
\mid\mathbf u,C)$ is similarly related to the second-order score
\cite{dytso2021}, \cite[Sec.~IV-A]{cai2026}:

Here the second-order score is the Hessian of the log density.
Equations~\eqref{eq:tweedie-mean} and \eqref{eq:tweedie-covariance}
express the channel moments through derivatives of the perturbed
channel density, avoiding direct evaluation of the posterior
integrals. We next learn the first-order score from channel
samples and use the resulting mean function to calculate the
required variance.

Let $S_\theta(\mathbf u,C)$ approximate the first-order score.
For a given perturbation covariance, score matching minimizes
the difference between this function and the score of
$q_{\bm\Sigma}^{\mathbb R}$. We use the covariance-weighted
objective

The unknown score prevents direct evaluation of this objective.
However, the Gaussian perturbation in \eqref{eq:colored-query}
has the known conditional score
$-\bm\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf u-\mathbf h_{\mathbb R})$.
Denoising score matching replaces the unknown score by this
conditional score \cite{vincent2011}, giving

The two objectives differ by a term independent of $\theta$.
At each fixed $C$, both are minimized by
$\nabla_{\mathbf u}\log q_{\bm\Sigma}^{\mathbb R}$ over
unrestricted score functions.

To obtain the channel estimate directly, we parameterize the
score through a mean function $f_\theta(\mathbf u,C)$ as
$S_\theta=\bm\Sigma^{-1}(f_\theta-\mathbf u)$.
Substituting this relation into \eqref{eq:denoising-score-objective}
gives the training loss

The expectation averages clean channels, perturbation covariances,
and Gaussian noise. For each fixed $C$, the conditional mean
$\mathbf m_{\mathbb R}(\mathbf u,C)$ minimizes this loss over
unrestricted mean functions. Thus, training with
\eqref{eq:first-loss} also learns the first-order score through
the above parameterization.

The denoiser must accommodate different input noise levels during
message passing. We therefore train over a range of perturbation
variances, as in \cite[Sec.~IV-B]{cai2026}. In the finite-dimensional
multi-frame model, the input errors can also be correlated.
To include such errors in training, we use colored perturbations
with covariance
$C=v(R_{\rm a}\otimes\I_N\otimes R_{\rm c})$ in
antenna--output--input order and condition the network on $C$
\cite[Sec.~III-B]{shastri2022}. The covariance factors and the
sampling law for $v$ are specified in
Section~\ref{sec:training-settings}.

Reshaping the real and imaginary outputs of $f_\theta$ defines
the complex mean map $F_\theta(R,C)$. For the scalar-variance
message in \eqref{eq:pseudo-awgn}, this map is evaluated at
$C=v\I_D$. The network architecture and preconditioning are given in
Section~\ref{sec:network-settings}.

The joint posterior moments in \eqref{eq:exact-local-moments}
require the channel variance as well as its mean. Differentiating
\eqref{eq:tweedie-mean} with respect to $\mathbf u$ at fixed $C$
gives the output-by-input Jacobian
$\mathbf J_m=\partial\mathbf m_{\mathbb R}/\partial\mathbf u
=\I_{2D}+\bm\Sigma\nabla_{\mathbf u}^2
\log q_{\bm\Sigma}^{\mathbb R}(\mathbf u)$.
Multiplying by $\bm\Sigma$ on the right and using
\eqref{eq:tweedie-covariance} yields
\cite[Prop.~1]{dytso2021}

The trace sums real and imaginary variances, so division by $D$
gives the variance per complex coordinate. At $C=v\I_D$, this
reduces to $\tau^\star=v\operatorname{div}\mathbf m_{\mathbb R}/(2D)$.
Thus, the scalar variance required by the receiver can be obtained
from derivatives of the same conditional-mean function.

We approximate this quantity by replacing the exact mean with
$f_\theta$ and estimating its derivative trace through Monte Carlo
finite differences \cite[Sec.~V-B]{metzler2014}. For independent
random sign vectors $\mathbf z_\ell$ with
$\E[\mathbf z_\ell\mathbf z_\ell^{\mathsf T}]=\I_{2D}$, set
$\mathbf w_\ell=\bm\Sigma^{1/2}\mathbf z_\ell$. The estimate is

Both evaluations hold $C$ fixed and differentiate the complete mean
map, including the preconditioning in \eqref{eq:mean-preconditioning}.
Evaluating \eqref{eq:derivative-trace} at $C=v\I_D$ supplies
the conditional variance estimates for the message updates.
Their use in the receiver is described in Section~\ref{sec:overall}, and the
finite-difference settings are given in
Section~\ref{sec:receiver-settings}.

The preceding calculations provide the conditional channel mean
and variance. The remaining quantity for joint estimation is
the activity probability, which depends on the likelihoods of
the active and inactive hypotheses. Rewriting
\eqref{eq:local-activity} gives

The inactive likelihood $q_{0,v}$ is known, whereas $q_{1,v}$
involves the channel integral in \eqref{eq:query-densities}.
Only their ratio is needed in \eqref{eq:activity-log-odds}.
We estimate this ratio directly by binary classification
\cite{menon2016}, using samples from the full channel prior.

To construct the two classes, draw $a\in\{0,1\}$ with
$\Pr(a=1)=\pi_{\rm tr}=1/2$. For $a=1$, generate
$R=H+W$ with $H\sim q_{\rm tr}$; for $a=0$, generate $R=W$.
In both classes, $\vect(W)\sim\CN(\mathbf0,v\I_D)$
independently of $H$, and $v$ has the same sampling law.
The resulting class-conditional densities are precisely those in
\eqref{eq:query-densities}. We learn a logit by minimizing the
binary cross-entropy loss

At the population optimum over unrestricted logits, this loss
recovers the training posterior log odds:

Subtracting the training prior log odds therefore estimates the
log density ratio \cite[Sec.~4.2]{menon2016}. With
$F_k=F_\theta(R_k,v\I_D)$, substitution into
\eqref{eq:activity-log-odds} gives the receiver activity probability

where $\logit a=\log[a/(1-a)]$ and
$\sigmoid b=(1+e^{-b})^{-1}$. The activity prior $\rho$ enters
through this Bayes correction, separately from the learned density
ratio.

The classifier uses the observation together with $F_k$, so its
features include the channel
estimate obtained from the learned prior. We first train the
denoiser and then hold it fixed while training the classifier.
The frozen denoiser output is a deterministic function of $R$
and $v$, which preserves the population relation in \eqref{eq:ideal-logit}.
Together, the denoiser, its derivative estimate, and the classifier
provide approximations to the channel moments and activity
probability required in Section~\ref{sec:joint-denoising}. Both networks
remain fixed during online inference.
